questions.q: On the night the Kali Yuga began, how many of the six bodies sat within 10° of the zero point, and what arc held all six?
questions.do: In Case 1, keep Days from the Kali Yuga epoch at 0 and Zero at Revati (ζ Piscium) selected. Read the two summary tiles.
questions.a: 4 of 6 sit within 10°, and all six fit in a 40.7° arc. Mercury (−21.3°) and Saturn (−32.7°) trail behind, so it was a loose gathering, not one point.

questions.q: What changes if you measure from a different zero point?
questions.do: In Case 1, click Zero opposite Spica (Lahiri) and read the planet list and both summary tiles.
questions.a: Every planet shifts by about 4° (the Sun goes from −5.7° to −9.7°). Now only 3 of 6 are within 10°. The arc holding all six stays 40.7°, because moving the zero point does not move the planets against each other.

questions.q: How much does the date of the Vedanga Jyotisha change if the author meant a point 10° away from the star α Delphini?
questions.do: In Case 4, move Where in Dhanishtha the author meant to +10.0°, then to −10.0°, and read Winter solstice at that point in.
questions.a: At the star: 1393 BCE. At +10°: 2109 BCE. At −10°: 677 BCE. The solstice drifts about 1° every 72 years, so 10° moves the date by about 720 years.

questions.q: The Crab Nebula's gas, run backwards, points to about 1091 CE, not 1054. Why the gap?
questions.do: Read the verdict under Case 3 · A guest star becomes the Crab Nebula.
questions.a: The filaments are not coasting. The pulsar's wind has been pushing them faster ever since, so a straight-line rewind comes up short, about 40 years after 1054. The 1054 Chinese record fixes the true age.

questions.q: Old eclipse records show the Earth's spin is slowing. How much shorter was a day in Aryabhata's time than in 1820?
questions.do: In Case 2, read the result for 136 BCE first. Then set Year to 499 CE and read The day was shorter than in 1820 by.
questions.a: For the Babylonian eclipse of 136 BCE, a steady-Earth clock is off by 3.34 hours and the track lands 4,706 km west. In 499 CE the day was about 26.8 ms (about 27 ms) shorter than in 1820. That is real, but far too small for a naked-eye astronomer or a water clock to notice.
